title: The Vijayanagara Empire
description: An illustrated map of the Vijayanagara Empire, from its founding on the Tungabhadra in 1336, through Krishnadevaraya’s reign and the battle of Talikota in 1565, to its last capitals and the rediscovery of Hampi.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Vijayanagara Empire from 1327 to 1646, and the ruins of Hampi
note: Based on inscriptions, the excavated city, Persian and Portuguese travellers and chroniclers, and Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and Sanskrit literature; each chapter says which it follows. The founding story is tradition, and the founders’ origins are debated. Army sizes and death tolls from chronicles are given as they state them and are disputed. The map is stylised and not to scale, and the Powers areas are painted loosely: borders shifted constantly, and the nayakas often ruled on their own.

steps.title: Delhi comes south
steps.text: In the 1320s the armies of Muhammad bin Tughluq, Sultan of Delhi, reach deep into the south. In 1327 they destroy Kampili, a small kingdom on the Tungabhadra river that had sheltered a rebel. Later accounts say two brothers who served Kampili, Harihara and Bukka, were taken to Delhi; historians still debate their origins.
steps.today: Today: Kampili, a town near Hampi, Karnataka, India.

steps.title: A city of victory
steps.text: Tradition says Harihara and Bukka founded a new city on the south bank of the Tungabhadra in 1336, blessed by the sage Vidyaranya. One story has hunting dogs chased off by a brave hare, a sign that the ground bred courage. They named it Vijayanagara, ‘city of victory’, among boulder hills sacred to the god Virupaksha.
steps.today: Today: Hampi, Vijayanagara district, Karnataka.

steps.title: From sea to sea
steps.text: In 1343 the last great Hoysala king, Veera Ballala III, is killed fighting the Madurai Sultanate, and the Sangama brothers take over his lands. In 1346 the five brothers gather at Sringeri to make a grant to its monastery (matha), celebrating rule ‘from the eastern to the western sea’, a proud claim not yet true.
steps.today: Today: Sringeri, Chikkamagaluru district, Karnataka.

steps.title: The Bahmani rival
steps.text: In 1347 Delhi’s nobles in the Deccan rebel and found the Bahmani Sultanate, ruled from Gulbarga. Between the two new powers lies the Raichur doab, fertile land between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers. For two centuries they fight over it, nearly every generation. Firishta, a later Persian chronicler, gives huge death tolls; historians treat them as exaggerated.
steps.today: Today: Kalaburagi, Karnataka; the Bahmani fort and mosque survive.

steps.title: The conquest of Madurai
steps.text: Bukka I’s son Kumara Kampana marches south, conquers the Madurai Sultanate and restores worship at temples such as Srirangam. His wife Gangadevi tells the story in a Sanskrit poem, the Conquest of Madurai (Madhuravijayam), in which a goddess hands Kampana a sword. The sultanate is gone by 1378, and Vijayanagara rules almost the whole south.
steps.today: Today: Madurai, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: A Persian envoy’s wonder
steps.text: Abdur Razzaq, envoy of the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh, sails to Calicut, then travels to Deva Raya II’s capital in 1443. The eye has never seen such a place, he writes, describing seven rings of walls, bazaars of jewels and flowers, and the nine-night Mahanavami festival, with elephants, dancers and fireworks before the king.
steps.today: Today: the ruins of Hampi’s royal centre.

steps.title: Invasions and usurpers
steps.text: After Deva Raya II the Sangama line weakens. Kapilendra, Gajapati king of Odisha, pushes far down the east coast, and the Bahmanis take Goa. Saluva Narasimha, governor at Chandragiri, drives back the invaders and in 1485 takes the throne himself. In 1505 Vira Narasimha of the Tuluva family seizes it in turn.
steps.today: Today: Chandragiri fort, near Tirupati, Andhra Pradesh.

steps.title: Krishnadevaraya crowned
steps.text: In 1509 Vira Narasimha’s half-brother Krishnadevaraya is crowned. He rules for twenty years and becomes the empire’s most celebrated king: general, poet and builder. His minister Saluva Timmarasu, remembered as Appaji, guides him. In 1510 he adds a gateway tower (gopuram) to the Virupaksha temple, the shrine at the heart of Hampi.
steps.today: Today: the Virupaksha temple, Hampi, still in worship.

steps.title: Horses and the Portuguese
steps.text: War horses do not breed well in the south, so every army depends on Arabian and Persian horses shipped across the sea. Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut in 1498, and in 1510 Afonso de Albuquerque takes Goa from Bijapur. Vijayanagara and the Portuguese become trading partners, and Goa’s horses flow inland to the capital.
steps.today: Today: Old Goa, a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The Kalinga campaigns
steps.text: Krishnadevaraya turns on the Gajapatis. He takes the hill fort of Udayagiri in 1514 and Kondavidu in 1515, then marches up the coast and raises a victory pillar at Potnuru. Peace follows. Tradition says he married a daughter of the Gajapati king Prataparudra, though accounts disagree about her name and the marriage.
steps.today: Today: Kondavidu fort, Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh.

steps.title: The battle of Raichur
steps.text: In 1520 Krishnadevaraya besieges Raichur, and Ismail Adil Shah of Bijapur comes to relieve it. Vijayanagara wins a great battle by the Krishna, and Portuguese musketeers help take the fort. The chronicler Fernão Nunes gives the king’s army as more than 700,000 men, surely an exaggeration. The doab is Vijayanagara’s again.
steps.today: Today: Raichur fort, Karnataka.

steps.title: As large as Rome
steps.text: The Portuguese visitor Domingo Paes finds the capital ‘as large as Rome, and very beautiful to the sight’, and calls it the best provided city in the world. He describes markets of rice, rubies and pearls, and a king who rises before dawn to exercise. Modern estimates of the population, often about half a million, are debated.
steps.today: Today: Hampi Bazaar, the old market street before the Virupaksha temple.

steps.title: Poets at court
steps.text: Krishnadevaraya writes in Sanskrit and Telugu. His Telugu poem Amuktamalyada retells the life of the poet-saint Andal and declares Telugu the finest language of the land. Eight great poets (ashtadiggajas) are said to grace his court, among them Allasani Peddana. Folk tales add the witty jester Tenali Rama; those stories are tradition.
steps.today: Today: Krishnadevaraya’s poems are still read in Telugu classrooms.

steps.title: Temples of stone
steps.text: The kings pour wealth into temples. At the Vitthala temple a shrine to the bird Garuda is carved as a stone chariot (ratha), and the hall’s slender pillars ring when tapped. Krishnadevaraya gives lavishly to the god at Tirumala, where bronze statues of him and his two queens, Chinna Devi and Tirumala Devi, still stand.
steps.today: Today: the stone chariot is on India’s 50 rupee note.

steps.title: The nayakas
steps.text: Krishnadevaraya dies in 1529; his brother Achyuta Deva Raya succeeds him, and a great temple at Hampi is built in his name in 1534. The empire is held together by nayakas, military chiefs who govern lands in return for troops and tribute. In Madurai and Thanjavur new nayaka houses take root, loyal for now.
steps.today: Today: the Achyutaraya temple ruins, Hampi.

steps.title: Rama Raya’s gamble
steps.text: From 1542 the young king Sadashiva reigns in name, while Aliya Rama Raya, Krishnadevaraya’s son-in-law (aliya), rules in fact. He plays the five Deccan Sultanates against one another, joining first one and then another in their wars. His armies sack Ahmadnagar, and the sultans come to fear him more than they distrust each other.
steps.today: Today: Vijayapura, Karnataka, the old Bijapur.

steps.title: The battle of Talikota
steps.text: Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar unite against Vijayanagara. Their armies meet Rama Raya’s south of the Krishna, near Rakkasagi and Tangadagi, a battle named after nearby Talikota. The aged regent is captured and beheaded. Some accounts say two Muslim commanders in his army changed sides; historians disagree. His army breaks and flees.
steps.today: Today: the villages of Rakkasagi and Tangadagi, Vijayapura district.

steps.title: The sack of the city
steps.text: Rama Raya’s brother Tirumala flees south with the king and, say Portuguese writers, the treasury loaded on hundreds of elephants. The victors plunder the capital for months, burning palaces and smashing temples. In 1567 the Italian merchant Cesare Federici finds the houses standing but empty, with tigers and wild beasts living in them.
steps.today: Today: the burnt platforms of Hampi’s royal centre.

steps.title: Penukonda and the Aravidus
steps.text: Tirumala crowns himself at Penukonda, a hill fortress to the south-east, and founds the Aravidu dynasty, the empire’s fourth. The old capital is never rebuilt. The empire still has a king, an army and great nayakas under it, but the Deccan Sultanates now hold the Raichur doab, and the nayakas grow ever more independent.
steps.today: Today: Penukonda, Sri Sathya Sai district, Andhra Pradesh.

steps.title: Venkata II at Chandragiri
steps.text: Venkata II, the last strong emperor, moves the court to Chandragiri, safer from the sultanates. Jesuit missionaries visit him, and he holds his nayakas mostly in check. In 1610 Raja Wodeyar of Mysore takes Srirangapatna from the imperial governor, the start of the Mysore kingdom. Venkata’s death in 1614 brings a ruinous civil war.
steps.today: Today: the Raja Mahal at Chandragiri, now a museum.

steps.title: A grant to the English
steps.text: In 1639 Damarla Venkatadri Nayaka, a local chief under the emperor Venkata III, grants a strip of coast to Francis Day of the English East India Company. There the English build Fort St George, around which Madras grows. His successor, Sriranga III, confirms the grant in 1645: one of the empire’s last acts reaches far into the future.
steps.today: Today: Fort St George, Chennai, seat of Tamil Nadu’s government.

steps.title: The last emperor
steps.text: Armies of Bijapur and Golconda overrun the last imperial lands in the 1640s; Vellore falls about 1646. Sriranga III, the last emperor, wanders between the courts of his former nayakas seeking help and dies in exile, by most accounts in the 1670s. The nayakas of Mysore, Madurai, Thanjavur and Keladi rule on as kings.
steps.today: Today: Vellore Fort, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: A forgotten empire
steps.text: After Tipu Sultan’s fall in 1799, the surveyor Colin Mackenzie maps the ruins at Hampi and gathers inscriptions and local histories. In 1856 Alexander Greenlaw photographs them. In 1900 Robert Sewell publishes A Forgotten Empire, translating the chronicles of Paes and Nunes, and the city of victory returns to the history books.
steps.today: Today: Mackenzie’s collections are in Chennai and London.

steps.title: World Heritage
steps.text: In 1986 the ruins of Hampi become a World Heritage Site: more than 1,600 surviving structures across some 4,000 hectares of boulder hills, temples, bazaars, aqueducts and palace platforms. Excavations still uncover the royal centre, and the Virupaksha temple has never stopped holding worship. Each year the Hampi Utsav festival recalls the old Mahanavami.
steps.today: Today: the Group of Monuments at Hampi, Karnataka.

items.name: Nayaka kingdoms
items.role: Military governors under the emperor who become kings in all but name as the empire weakens.

items.name: Kingdom of Mysore
items.role: A former vassal that takes Srirangapatna in 1610 and grows into a major kingdom.

items.name: English East India Company
items.role: English traders granted a strip of coast by a Vijayanagara nayaka.

items.name: Harihara I
items.role: Founder of the Sangama dynasty
items.text: The eldest of the five sons of Sangama, Harihara is remembered as the empire’s first king, though he never takes an imperial title. With his brother Bukka he wins the Hoysala lands and holds the line against the new Bahmani Sultanate. Whether the brothers were Kannada or Telugu by origin is still argued.

items.name: Bukka I
items.role: Co-founder and second king
items.text: Harihara’s brother and successor, Bukka fights the Bahmanis and sends his son Kumara Kampana to conquer the Madurai Sultanate. By his death the empire covers nearly all of the south. Later inscriptions praise him as protector of all faiths, and one records him settling a dispute between Jains and Vaishnavas.

items.name: Vidyaranya
items.role: Sage and head of the Sringeri monastery, in tradition the empire’s founder-guide
items.text: Tradition makes Vidyaranya the guru who inspired Harihara and Bukka to found the city. He headed the Sringeri monastery and is often identified with the scholar Madhava, though historians debate whether they were the same man, and the earliest records of the empire do not mention his role.

items.name: Gangadevi
items.role: Poet and wife of Kumara Kampana
items.text: A princess and poet, Gangadevi wrote the Madhuravijayam, a Sanskrit poem on her husband’s conquest of Madurai. It mixes history with legend and describes the ruined temples of the south. Lost for centuries, the manuscript was found and printed in 1916.

items.name: Deva Raya II
items.role: The greatest Sangama king
items.text: Deva Raya II modernised his army by recruiting Muslim horse archers, and Firishta says he gave them land and a mosque in the capital. His court welcomed Abdur Razzaq. In 1443, the envoy reports, the king survived an assassination plot by a close relative at a feast.

items.name: Abdur Razzaq Samarqandi
items.role: Envoy of the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh
items.text: Sent from Herat to the ruler of Calicut, Abdur Razzaq went on to Vijayanagara in 1443. His travel account, part of a larger Persian history, is among the most vivid descriptions of the city at its height, from its walls and markets to the king’s festival.

items.name: Krishnadevaraya
items.role: Tuluva emperor, the empire’s most celebrated king
items.text: Undefeated in battle, Krishnadevaraya wins back the Raichur doab, humbles the Gajapatis and keeps peace with the Portuguese. A poet in Telugu and Sanskrit, he gathers great writers at his court and endows temples from Hampi to Tirumala. Kannada and Telugu speakers alike remember him as their own.

items.name: Domingo Paes
items.role: Portuguese traveller
items.text: A Portuguese visitor, probably a trader from Goa, Paes spent time at the capital around 1520 to 1522. His long, admiring account describes the king, the festivals, the markets and the palaces. It survives in a single copy, bound together with the chronicle of Fernão Nunes.

items.name: Fernão Nunes
items.role: Portuguese horse trader and chronicler
items.text: Nunes lived at Vijayanagara in the 1530s, trading horses. He wrote a history of the kings from the founding to his own day, including the most detailed account of the battle of Raichur, with army sizes historians treat as inflated.

items.name: Allasani Peddana
items.role: Telugu poet at Krishnadevaraya’s court
items.text: Peddana is honoured as ‘grandfather of Telugu poetry’ (Andhra Kavitapitamaha). His Manucharitramu, the tale of a Brahmin who flies to the Himalaya and resists a celestial nymph, set the style of the great Telugu court epics (prabandhas). Tradition says the king himself helped carry his palanquin.

items.name: Tenali Rama
items.role: Poet, and the clever jester of folk tales
items.text: Tenali Ramakrishna was a real Telugu poet, but he is best known from folk stories, in which he outwits rivals, swindlers and even the king. Those tales are tradition, retold across India in comics, schoolbooks and cartoons, and are not evidence of what happened at court.

items.name: Aliya Rama Raya
items.role: Regent of the empire
items.text: Krishnadevaraya’s son-in-law, from the Aravidu family, Rama Raya ruled for over twenty years in the name of Sadashiva. A skilled but overbearing diplomat, he drew the Deccan Sultanates into an alliance against him. Captured at Talikota, he was beheaded, by Firishta’s account on the order of Hussain Nizam Shah.

items.name: Venkata II
items.role: Aravidu emperor
items.text: Venkata II held the shrinking empire together for almost thirty years, ruling from Penukonda and then Chandragiri. He beat back attacks from Golconda and welcomed Jesuits to his court. He died without a son, and the fight over his throne broke the empire’s last strength.

items.name: Colin Mackenzie
items.role: Surveyor, later first Surveyor General of India
items.text: A Scottish army engineer, Mackenzie surveyed Mysore after 1799 and made the first plan of the ruins at Hampi. With Indian assistants he gathered thousands of inscriptions, manuscripts and local histories, a collection still used by historians of the south.

items.name: Robert Sewell
items.role: Civil servant and historian
items.text: A British official in the Madras Presidency, Sewell wrote A Forgotten Empire (1900), the first full history of Vijayanagara in English. It includes his translations of the Portuguese chronicles of Paes and Nunes, and brought the empire to a wide audience.
